77.t: First awareness of gangsters at the Burnham Inn; how they treated artists
77.s: Burnham was where she first knew she was working for gangsters; they protected artists, paid well and ran most clubs through fronts, and she will say only good things about them.
77.ch: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
77.q: No, because they were all -- they were so good to me that I have absolutely nothing to say about them but something good. Nothing.

77.t: Wild Chicago night life and after-hours spots
77.s: Clubs closed at midnight but after-hours spots stayed open; sporting women and con men did not bother anyone and strangers returned dropped money.
77.q: Oh, well, for instance you'd close at 12:00 o'clock now, then you could go on down to the after-hour spots, and stay until -- hours. Then you got ready to go home, sometimes 9:00, 10:00 o'clock, later than that. As long as you wanted to. They didn't close. No, they didn't close. And nobody bothered…

77.t: Royal Garden, the Sunset and working for Joe Glazer
77.s: In Chicago she moved from the Royal Garden to the Sunset with Louis; she describes Glazer, who managed sports figures, as kind and generous despite gangster ties.
77.q: If you haven't, I'm going to ask somebody. I know I worked and then I went over to the Royal Garden. And then from the Royal Garden I went to the Sunset. All this is in Chicago.

77.t: Pickpockets working downtown near the depots
77.s: They worked downtown near the stations, not uptown clubs, and came to the club to spend money and give her lots of tips.
77.q: Out. They'd all go downtown, downtown. They wouldn't pick pockets uptown. They all go downtown where most of the businessmen or travelling people -- they hung out more or less around the stations. We called it the depots, up north, but dee-pots, down south. And they would rob those people.

77.t: The confidence men Big and Little Harry, and how they protected her
77.s: Harry Merrill and Little Harry conned people, once her stepfather out of his grocery, but taught her how not to be turned into a bad girl.
77.q: So then they had Harry Merrill. They called him Big Harry. He was a confidence man. And Little Harry was a confidence man. They were -- wouldn't exactly call them pimps because they made their own money by confidencing people, you see. In fact they confidenced my stepfather out of his grocery, out…

77.t: The gangster-run Burnham Inn and the man dead when the lights came on
77.s: She made a fortune at the Burnham Inn in Burnham, Illinois, where once the lights went out during her song and a dead man lay there when they came back.
77.ch: New Orleans musicians, recordings and radio
77.q: That's right. And then now, Chris, when I worked in Chicago, there was a place called the Burnham Inn in Burnham, Illinois, and you used to -- we -- a lot of the people used to go out to Burnham, because that was owned by the gangsters.

67.t: The Pekin Inn and mob control of Chicago clubs
67.s: The Pekin Inn was a Chinese restaurant where musicians gathered after hours; he guesses gangsters ran most Chicago clubs.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: It was a Chinese place, yes. It was a joint where the musicians would gather there quite a lot and they would have a few players, sometimes would play the Pekin Inn. But it was mostly a Chinese -- where you get good Chinese food.

67.t: Capone men taking over the Dreamland for the night
67.s: He was once in a Dreamland raid, and Capone people closed the club for private nights and tipped the band, who played until sunup.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Well, no, I don't think they affected, and I was in a raid once in the Dreamland, that's all I remember and nothing happened, you know, money would straighten out everything in those days. But I was in a raid in Chicago, and I remember the Capone -- members of the Capone organization come in all…

67.t: Gangsters as the Dreamland's big spenders and tippers
67.s: Cafes were supported by gangsters, who took over the night and left hundreds of dollars in tips.
67.q: That was one of the only times we made any money at the Dreamland was when the gangsters came in here. And they would spend money, that was the only times they

67.t: Lorraine Gardens, the Dreamland crowd and bootleg liquor
67.s: The Lorraine was lower class; the Dreamland drew downtown people, pimps and gangsters, with concealed bootleg whiskey and raids.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Oh, yes. Oh, yes, it was, sort of lower class during that time. That was when the Dreamland was very popular, it was lower class type of a place.

56.t: Al Capone coming into the clubs
56.s: Capone visited the Plantation with guns on the table and gave Ory good liquor.
56.q: I knew Al. Hmm? Sure. You did know him? Yeah, all the boys, yeah. Yeah? Did you work with him? Gang, yeah. No, I didn't wake for him. He used to come in the club. Uh-huh. Plantation all the time. The plantation, huh? They used to bring him liquor. Good liquor. The guys, they were very nice to me.…

56.t: Rival gangs in the club and a shooting
56.s: Gangs sat on opposite sides; Ory once took cover behind a kitchen stove.
56.q: everybody's dead at a good time they all kept their guns on the table were you ever in the place where they were shooting did it ever happen to you once in sunset started shooting I don't know who was were you playing there or just yeah you were playing at the sunset I found myself behind the stove…

56.t: Boyd Atkins's band and the St. Valentine's Day massacre
56.s: Ory was with Boyd Atkins and mistaken for a gunman on the morning of the Moran killings.
56.q: no I was with boyd asking band boyd asking that's your call the vagabond they call it i thought you were blowing it was you is oh it was formerly louie's band you know uh-huh but no one yeah i was on the air when uh the morning that uh moran gang was uh murdered you know i got off in Cicero to go…

752.t: Chicago in the twenties: Capone, tips and the Rex
752.s: Mugsy on money, gangsters in the clubs, Friars Inn and the Valentine's Day massacre.
752.q: When did you make those records with Mackenzie Condon? That was a little later, huh? Uh-huh. I just made one record with Eddie and the... It was one record then? Yeah. Be some changes made, found a new baby. That's the only one I made. I didn't make sugar and all that. You mean you just made two…

752.t: Chicago, St. Louis spots and Dean O'Banion
752.s: Pops on Chicago and St. Louis as musician towns, then Mugsy on a fight with the gangster Dean O'Banion.
752.q: Chicago was the number one spot for musicians in the St. Louis. Chicago was St. Louis. They had both fun on in the St. Louis. But then they, and the general, they had St. Louis over. Then you go to the Beardstown, Beardstown, man. Quite a few spots. Used to take us there. Where was that? Illinois.…

924.t: Tick Young's Cabaret and the trumpet-like jazz sax
924.s: Jones describes his months at Tick Young's, and the horn he played that sounded like a trumpet, earning him the nickname second Louis Armstrong, versus the clarinet-like nose whistle.
924.q: Oh, I stayed at Tick Young's, I guess. Enough to stay in jail all the time. Back and forth with the gangsters. Yeah, I stayed there about five, six months after Tick Young's.

924.t: Chicago white clubs, gangsters and pay
924.s: Jones played white nightclubs and theaters, run by gangsters, never colored clubs. He made $150-200 a night and talks about the Haymarket.
924.q: I played in white night club, played in white theaters, played in the finest places you could find from the show boat in St. Louis on down. Played all over the country.

400.t: Working in Capone-run clubs: Boyd Atkins, Ed Depappa and mean Ralph Capone
400.s: Hinton lists Capone-family clubs that used all-black entertainment, with Boyd Atkins's band, and contrasts brutal Ralph with Al, whom he calls a nice man to work for.
400.ch: Capone's Chicago, the union and hired by Cab
400.q: Yeah, Boyd Atkins. Al Capone had the Cotton Club on Cicero and then they begin to branch out. This guy Ed Depappa had the club where… a small club on the north side where Eddie South was. And Ralph Capone, Al Capone‟s brother opened a club downtown in Chicago.

400.t: The Jones brothers, policy racket and Hinton's uncle Matt
400.s: The Jones boys ran the Harlem in the Bronx policy game, with Hinton's uncle as treasurer, until gangsters moved in and they went to Mexico.
400.ch: Eddie South, high school and the South Side scene
400.q: That‟s right, oh, yeah. They got in the rackets. They couldn‟t do anything as long as their father was living because he was president of the National Baptist Convention, which is a big thing. My mother was his secretary and assistant and all that, and everything. So when he died those boys were…

95.t: Ma Rainey in Chicago, her gold pieces and young lovers
95.s: She knew Ma Rainey, saw her robbed of her gold-piece necklace at her brother's house, and says Ma took young lovers.
95.q: I knew her well -- as well as I know (unintelligible) "It's been raining all night and (inaudible) (Singing) I ain't going away no more." Ma Rainey said (unintelligible) --

95.t: Ma Rainey robbed of her gold pieces again
95.s: She retells Ma Rainey being robbed and her brother stammering to her, placing it when she was not yet twenty.
95.q: Yeah, I would, but I say at the time I met Ma , at the time I . See, that's what I'm talking about. At the time I . (Unintelligible) she got held up on 25th Street, come in and crying, go in and tell my brother, said, "Mr. , (unintelligible)." And my brother stammers when he talks, my brother say,…

275.t: Prohibition-era Chicago: working for Al Capone at the Triangle
275.s: He played the Triangle nightclub in Chicago, owned by Al Capone.
275.q: During my time of show business and back in the Prohibition days, I appeared at the various nightclubs there. And I happened to be appearing at the Triangle nightclub there, which at that time was one of the popular nightclubs. And the very well-known gentleman owned the place was Al Capone. And I…

12.s: A gangster's bomb goes off at midnight in the club; audience stays and the band plays on.
12.q: He was supposed to play at the Royal Garden and burn down. And we waited and went into the plantation profane. It was a beautiful place. Uh-huh. Then they hold a band there. What was it like then? Was there much burning and explosions and all that? No, those were the gangsters. I remember one night…

8.t: The Dixieland band and the rough Pozzonia club on Madison and Paulina
8.s: Garland recalls a rough west-side club with gangsters, where he played opposite a white Dixieland five without trumpet, with a kazoo-playing drummer called Monkey.
8.q: Lorenzo Teo, you see. Was playing clarinet. I played bass. Then the Dixon Land, the original Dixon Land, uh, jazz band from New Orleans, white boys, Dixon Land 5, we played on Madison and Paulina on the west side, the Osonia. They in one corner was another corner.

881.t: Gangsters and the clubs: Capone's brother and Walter Barnes
881.s: He worked for Capone's brother Ralph and Ed Fox, recalls Walter Barnes and his fatal tour, and says known gangsters frequented the clubs.
881.q: You didn't see him? No, I didn't know him until later on, you know. Yeah, it was maybe a year or so before he was killed, assassinated. But he could have, and I worked for it. I worked for Capone's brother, Ralph. Yeah, the syndicate had the grand tier, so the Hood Heinz bands. A fellow by the name…

15.t: Al Capone's circle, the Grand Terrace syndicate and Joe Fosco
15.s: Howard went to school with Capone's brother, grew up in an Italian neighborhood, and says the syndicate was behind the Grand Terrace.
15.q: Yeah. They had some kind of business. Now, I saw a truck pass about two years ago. I don't remember what it was. It had Capone on the truck. Or they strictly legitimate. His brother? Yeah. Was he always? I think so. I never heard anything about him being messed up. Just he and Hal was the two that…

68.t: Lucky Millinder, Tab Smith and Al Capone
68.s: Tate says Lucky paid more than Basie and tells how Capone gave him a band.
68.q: Might be in Savoy Ballroom, 1940, 1939. It might have been the Savoy Ballroom. It might have been 1939 but it says 1940. Edison’s here. Ed Lewis, Buck Clayton. Vic Dickenson, Dickie Wells, Dan Minor. There’s some heavy cats in there. Freddie, Tab Smith, Tab always loved, music-wise he loved Basie’s…

108.t: How Lucky Millinder got his name
108.s: Stories of Millinder's luck, his Chicago youth and admiration for Capone.
108.q: It’s my understanding that he had had some really close scrapes on many occasions, and he always managed to come out smelling like a rose. Somebody said, “He’s lucky,” and that name stuck with him. I also understand that when he was a youngster, he used to run errands for Al Capone in Chicago.…

226.t: Playing at gunpoint for gangsters in Cicero
226.s: At the end of a night the gangsters made the band play another show at gunpoint and tipped each man $100.
226.ch: Depression-era Chicago: jobs, marriage, first bands
226.q: In Chicago, outside of – the south side of Chicago – not the south side. I mean the west side, way west, in Cicero, which is adjoining to Chicago, like a suburb, there was – gangsters had

374.t: Gangsters and corrupt police around the music; being cased in Chicago
374.s: Daughtry raises the gangster and police element in jazz; Russell recalls being stopped by men in cars and claiming Spanish and Irish nationality.
374.q: Yes sir. You’d be walking down the street. By that time I had sensed – I had developed a really sharp sense of when I was being cased. They would be two guys in a car, wearing hats, and they’d be moving slowly behind you. When you’d go to cross the street, they’d pull up in front of you and ask,…

26.t: Greer as the band's street-smart member
26.s: He knew night life better than Duke and the boys.
26.q: Yeah, I was the one. You know, it was a brand new whole world for Duke and the boys, it was a brand new world. They didn't know that stuff. But I was always involved in it from time beginning. I was involved in night life. I recorded. I was there. So I just picked up fast on all that stuff. And,…

0.t: Big Jim Colosimo's murder and the start of gangster Chicago
0.s: As a high school student working downtown he saw the beginnings of Capone's Mafia after Colosimo was assassinated; Prohibition did no harm to musicians' work.
0.ch: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
0.q: They were just beginning because I was working downtown during my vacation off from high school when this guy, Big Jim Collinsimo, had a place down on Wabash Avenue and I think it was around 23rd Street -- Big Jim Colisemo. Old Eddie South Softan worked a lot of them, worked there, and when they…

641.t: Gang wars, being shot, and meeting Capone
641.s: Joe was shot and beaten in the Berger-Shulman gang war while working the roadhouse, and met Al Capone and Purple Gang members there.
641.ch: Southern Illinois roadhouse and St. Louis
641.q: Well, this was a band that... When I left this roadhouse, I almost got killed. That's when I got shot for working in there. That's a story in itself. So in the meantime, I was in the hospital, because I had a bullet crease in my head, and a guy shot me through the knee here, and I got beat up, got…

120.t: The Silver Slipper on Chicago's South Side
120.s: The band opens at a big Chinese restaurant-club; the owner puts up Davison and his wife in an incense-filled flat; musicians' good times in Prohibition.
120.ch: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
120.q: It was a Chinese restaurant--- it was a fantastic one -- great hugh one. I remember it had palm trees all around the floor--

92.t: Gangsters and Chicago clubs: Capone's Radio Inn
92.s: Collins says gangster-owned clubs gave musicians work and sometimes shooting, and the Radio Inn was rumored to be Capone's.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Yeah, Wendell Phillips, yes. So after that, as I told you, I was working with my mother on the north side of Chicago. Gangsterland. And --

454.t: Ben Webster in Europe: dinner talk of gangsters
454.s: Webster cared about young musicians but he and McPherson talked only gangsters, Baby Bell and Lucky Luciano.
454.ch: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
454.q: He was a pimp in a gangster suit. (Unintelligible.) He was a cross between getting the bootleggers in the bootlegger days. Bootleg whisky and even narcotics, and the numbers over to the black people, to the Mafia.

76.t: Chicago gangster hangouts and the New Deal Club
76.s: Chicago meant seeing nothing; Zutty played Greenwood Gardens, a hangout of Capone's brother. He retells how Marge filled in at the New Deal Club, with Reuben Reeves, the gangsters' sons and no shooting.
76.ch: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
76.q: Like that New Deal in Chicago they had a lot of football players and all that hung out there. But they were gangsters really running it. But old Zutty's piano player called up two hours before time to go to work on Sunday that he couldn't make the Deal. Zutty was half afraid to go to work because…

455.t: Sixty dollars a week and escorts through Capone territory
455.s: The owner keeps the band at $60 and has armed men drive them through Capone's territory; later Teddy Wilson's car runs the north side.
455.ch: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
455.q: He said, "Now listen, you guys play the show better than anybody I've ever had here," and he says, "and you can play dance music." Now the job was paying us $60.00 a week a man.
